editor_output.issue_week: Calibration Fixture V2 -- synthetic data, not a real week

stories.headline: From the Desk of Mr. Pick Ems
stories.body:
Nobody announces a depth chart change. There's no press release when a backup starts eating into a starter's goal-line work, no chyron when a tight end quietly keeps a third of his emergency promotion after the starter comes back healthy. Teams just keep sending the same personnel out onto the field until the pattern is too obvious to call a coincidence.

This week gave me two of those. One is loud enough that I'm comfortable calling it early. The other is still arguing with itself — the kind of situation where the evidence tugs in two directions and I'd rather admit that than pretend it doesn't. I also had a couple of stories that looked, on the surface, like something was happening, and turned out on closer inspection to be exactly nothing. Those are worth mentioning too. Knowing what isn't a signal is half the job.

stories.headline: Keane's goal-line role has quietly taken over
stories.body:
The easy explanation was sitting right there: the incumbent back was banged up, so of course the backup picked up some goal-line work. Convenient, tidy, and it would have let me move on to something else.

Then the incumbent came back. Full practice, no restrictions, and the goal-line touches stayed where they'd gone — five of seven in the two games since. That's the detail that changes what this is. An injury explains a temporary shift. It doesn't explain a shift that outlives the injury.

What convinces me further is that this isn't happening in isolation. Snap share and red-zone targets moved with it, not just the raw touch count in one specific situation. When multiple signals move together and the shift survives the most obvious alternate explanation, I start treating it less like noise and more like a decision the team has already made and just hasn't said out loud.

The market has noticed something — the anytime-touchdown price has come in from +650 to +400 — but I'd stop short of calling this fully priced. Three games is real information. It isn't yet a settled depth chart, and I'm not going to pretend it is just because the story is a good one.

stories.headline: Osei's red-zone role held even after the starter's return
stories.body:
Here's a role change that's honest about its own limits, and I'd rather show you that than round it up into something cleaner.

With the starting tight end out, Osei's red-zone snap share nearly tripled. That much is unsurprising — backups play more when starters don't. What's more interesting is what happened when the starter came back: the share didn't fully revert. It dropped, but only partway, settling around double the original baseline.

That's a partial result, and I want to be clear it's a partial result. Some of this looks like it belongs to the injury and left when the injury did. Some of it looks like it's staying. The offensive coordinator has genuinely used more two-tight-end red-zone sets since the starter returned than he did in the season's first five weeks, which is the kind of supporting detail that makes me lean toward 'partly real' rather than 'entirely temporary.' The price moved modestly — not dramatically — which is about the right amount of market reaction for a signal that's itself only partly resolved.

stories.headline: Carolina's slot coverage: soft spot, or just tough opponents?
stories.body:
Two of Carolina's last three games have seen opposing slot receivers produce well above what you'd expect from their season-long numbers. That's a real pattern. What it means is a genuinely open question, and I think it's worth saying so plainly rather than picking a side to make a better paragraph.

The two elevated games both came against receivers ranked in the league's top eight at the position this season. The one game that came back at expectation came against a receiver ranked in the bottom half. That's consistent with a real coverage weakness — but it's just as consistent with Carolina simply having faced better players twice and a lesser one once. The data available doesn't separate those two stories from each other, and I don't think I should pretend it does.

I'm not ready to call this a defensive vulnerability. I'm also not ready to dismiss it. That's an uncomfortable place to leave a story, but it's the honest one.

cross_references.text: Keane's role shift, told in full above, is the cleaner version of the same question this section keeps returning to: how much evidence does it take before a pattern stops being a coincidence?
The week's most useful market read is really Keane's, covered above — a price that moved but likely hasn't finished moving.
The player most directly affected this week is Keane himself — see the Big One above.

editor_output.notes_for_human_reviewer:
This is Fixture V2 -- a new calibration test of the EPS-consumption behavior (Step 1, gate-reading, eps_scores copy-not-compute), not a reproduction or re-confirmation of the original two-round voice/structure calibration. That original fixture's content is unrecoverable per nfl/newsletter/README.md.

Gate/placement reasoning:
- Big One: FIXTURE-1 (Keane) was the only story with clear, high evidence + high composite value, and big_one_eligible=true. It also independently cleared watchlist_eligible=true, but per Step 2 it received its Big One treatment only -- I did not also place it in Watchlist, and pointed to it via cross_references from What Changed, Market Knows Something, and Who It Affects instead of writing any second full-body treatment for it. I was careful that none of those cross-reference sentences drifted into making the story's case at length -- each is a single pointer sentence.
- Watchlist: No section included. After removing FIXTURE-1 (already used as Big One), the only other watchlist_eligible=true story was FIXTURE-4 (Carolina slot defense), but I judged What Changed to be the better fit for it since it's a fully-formed, evidence-grounded (if unresolved) story rather than a thin/early one -- and per the "one Story Object, one primary treatment" rule it couldn't appear in both. With FIXTURE-4 placed in What Changed, no eligible candidates remained for Watchlist, so per the hard rule against structural symmetry I left it empty rather than force something in.
- Excluded entirely: FIXTURE-2 (Rhoads market stability) and FIXTURE-6 (Voss national-broadcast noise) both scored as confirmations of non-events -- low significance, low novelty, low tension, despite technically clearing big_one_eligible on evidence strength alone. Per the decision table ("low editorial value -> don't publish") and the instruction that a gate is necessary but not sufficient, I did not include either as stories. FIXTURE-3 (Denver red-zone) failed both gates and was excluded outright.
- Market Knows Something and Who It Affects: no independent story existed for either beyond what's already told in the Big One, so both sections carry only a cross-reference and no stories entry, per "no forced symmetry."
- Tasty Connection: left fully empty per the fixture's explicit note that no real TPE Picks data exists for this run -- I did not invent picks to fill it.
- eps_scores throughout are copied verbatim from each Story Object's upstream eps.dimensions and composite_score (mapped to eps_total) -- none were recomputed or adjusted by me.
- Flagging for review per the calibration scope: please specifically check the Carolina and Osei entries for whether the "genuinely unresolved / partial result" framing reads as revealed reasoning (intended) versus a hedge-heavy disclaimer (the anti-pattern called out in the voice section) -- these were the hardest calls to voice correctly under the new EPS-consumption constraints.

alternate_explanations.explanation: Team trailed by 17 points for most of the second half, which independently increases pass rate regardless of any real tendency shift
alternate_explanations.evidence: Game script shows a 17-point deficit from late in the 2nd quarter onward
alternate_explanations.test: Does the pass-rate shift hold once game-script (score differential) is accounted for?
alternate_explanations.result: Sample is too small (6 plays, one game state) to separate a real tendency shift from a game-script effect

confirmation.supporting_signals: None available beyond this single game
confirmation.contradicting_signals: 5-game baseline shows no trend in this direction prior to this game
confirmation.market_reaction: Not applicable — no market tied to this signal type

judgment.what_we_dont_know: Whether this reflects any real coaching tendency shift at all, given the sample can't be separated from game script
judgment.evidence_significance: Single-game sample confounded by game script means this cannot yet be distinguished from a normal trailing-team pass-rate spike

significance.rationale: One game, small sample, plausible confound — banded as small, not material

evidence_strength.rationale: NOT_TESTABLE status, single-game sample, real confound identified

betting_relevance.rationale: Would matter if real, but confound means interpretation shouldn't change yet

Watchlist also correctly fails since Evidence Strength (21) is below the Watchlist's own floor (25). fixtures.expected_stress_target: Both gates pass, which is correct — this is a legitimately uncertain but real story, not a weak one. The test is whether the Editor's prose honestly represents the UNRESOLVED status (two plausible explanations, genuinely can't distinguish yet) rather than picking a side and writing it as either 'Carolina has a real weakness' or 'this is nothing, just matchups.' Correct placement is primarily the Watchlist — 'something worth tracking, not yet confirmed either way.' UPDATED (duplicate-detection two-case rule): a brief cross-reference to this story from another section (e.g. naming it in passing while covering something else) is now explicitly correct, not a violation — but only ONE section may give it a full treatment with its own eps_scores/provenance block. A second full retelling of the same argument in a different section (e.g. an independent What Changed entry making the same case a second time) is the actual failure this fixture now tests for.

fixtures.headline: Osei's red-zone role held even after the starter's return

change.what_changed: Red-zone snap share increase, partial retention after starter's return

context.prior_baseline: 12% prior to starter's injury in Week 6

alternate_explanations.explanation: Starting TE's injury explains the entire increase, and the role should fully revert now that he's back
alternate_explanations.evidence: Starting TE missed Weeks 6-8 with a hamstring injury, returned Week 9

alternate_explanations.result: Osei's share dropped from 34% to 26% after the starter's return — a partial reversion, not a full one

judgment.what_we_dont_know: Whether the 26% level is the new stable rate or still settling

fixtures.expected_stress_target: Deliberately contrasts with Fixture 1's clean WEAKENED result — this one is WEAKENED but with a real contradicting signal (partial, not full, reversion), and the evidence_significance field explicitly says so. Tests whether the Editor's prose can express a partial, honest result ('some of this held, some of it didn't') rather than flattening every WEAKENED status into the same confident 'survived the test' framing Fixture 1 earns.
